lines.text: This is an H-block from Puma Punku, in Bolivia. Sharp edges. Flat faces. Inside corners at ninety degrees. And it is about fourteen hundred years old.
Millions of people have seen this stone online, with one claim attached. Laser cut. Machined. Built by visitors from another world.
So today we do something simple. We walk the site like engineers. Station by station, stone by stone, with a tape measure and the published survey data.
Laser-cut stones, or Tiwanaku genius? At the end, every claim goes on a scorecard. Let's start the survey.
Station one. The ground. Puma Punku sits on the Altiplano, about three thousand eight hundred and fifty metres above sea level, south of Lake Titicaca.
The name means Gate of the Puma. It was a T-shaped platform mound, faced with stone, about one hundred and sixty-seven metres by one hundred and seventeen.
It belonged to Tiwanaku, a great Andean city. At its peak, between about seven hundred and one thousand AD, ten to twenty thousand people lived in its core.
First measurement: age. Archaeologist Alexei Vranich dug down to the deepest, oldest layer of fill inside the mound and dated the organic material in it.
The result: between AD five hundred and thirty-six and six hundred. The stone buildings on top came after that. And under the fill, there was only sterile Ice Age sediment.
That matters, because one of the most repeated claims says Puma Punku is fifteen thousand years old. Keep that number in your pocket. We will test it later.
The first European to describe the site was Pedro Cieza de León, in fifteen forty-nine. The Spanish called what they saw inconceivable. Some walls and a gateway were still standing.
Then came five centuries of damage. Treasure hunters dug for gold. Stones were hauled away for churches, houses, and even railway ballast.
So the first rule of this survey: nothing is in its original position. As Vranich put it, there isn't a single stone in place.
Station two. The giants. On the east side lies the stone platform, the Plataforma Lítica, paved with the biggest slabs on the entire Tiwanaku site.
The largest slab measures about seven point eight metres long, five point two metres wide, and just over one metre thick.
Multiply by the density of red sandstone and you get roughly one hundred and thirty-one tonnes. The second largest comes in at about eighty-five tonnes.
Now compare that with the internet. Websites have listed four hundred and forty tons. One television series went all the way up to eight hundred.
Those big numbers came from early guesses that were corrected long ago. Real ceiling: about one hundred and thirty-one tonnes. And after the top two, the sizes drop sharply.
Where did the slabs come from? Geologists compared the stone, mineral by mineral and chemically, with quarries in the hills south of the site.
They found a match about ten to fifteen kilometres away. Later fieldwork pinned the main quarry down: a place called Kaliri, in the Kausani Valley.
Moving a hundred-tonne slab that far is hard work. Proposed methods include ropes of llama hide, ramps and inclined planes. The exact method is still debated.
But hard is not impossible. Other ancient builders moved far heavier stones. And here, the quarry is known, the stone is local, and the slabs are real sandstone.
Station three. The famous ones. The H-blocks. Grey volcanic andesite, carved into stepped H-shapes with crisp edges and deep recesses.
Each one has dozens of faces. Flat planes, sharp steps, and inside corners that really are close to a perfect right angle. This is the strongest card in the alien deck.
The claim on screen: every H-block is identical, so they must have been cut by one machine. Let's check that against the survey.

The architectural historians Jean-Pierre Protzen and Stella Nair measured them. Their finding: the blocks are so uniform they could be swapped with each other and still give a level surface and even joints.
But, quote, the blocks do not have the same dimensions. Similar. Standardised. Not identical. That points to a template and a skilled crew, not a machine.
Here is the clue that explains them. Tiwanaku carvers made scale models in stone, like the block called the Escritorio del Inca, a miniature of full-size architecture.
Many of these model stones exist in several copies. Protzen and Nair called it mass production. The H-blocks were prefabricated parts, made to fit into blind miniature gateways.
Second measurement on andesite: its origin. This harder, volcanic stone came from across Lake Titicaca, from the Copacabana Peninsula and Mount Ccapia, roughly ninety kilometres away.
And on the lake shore at a place called Iwawi, archaeologists found roughly shaped andesite blocks left behind on the route. Locals call them tired stones.
That is a transport trail with evidence on it. Quarry, half-finished blocks, a lake crossing, and the finished stones at Puma Punku.
Station four. The joints. How do these stones hold together without falling apart in earthquakes?
The blocks interlock like a puzzle. One trick: the top of a lower stone is cut at an angle, and the stone above is cut to match, so it cannot slide off.
Protzen and Nair also found a thin whitish coat, one to one and a half millimetres thick, on some stones. Possibly a mortar. So the famous no-mortar claim is not quite right either.
Now look at the tops. Little I-shaped and T-shaped slots run across the joints. These held metal cramps that locked neighbouring blocks together.
Chemical analysis shows the cramps are a rare bronze of copper, arsenic and nickel. In one canal at Puma Punku, the metal was poured molten, straight into the sockets.
And that technique is not alien. Ancient Greek builders used the same cramp shapes on the Erechtheion in Athens. The Egyptians used them too.
The same copper-arsenic-nickel bronze turns up in Tiwanaku artefacts across the region, from about AD six hundred to nine hundred. The metal fits the people and the period.
Station five. The tool test. If no machines were used, can a human with ancient tools actually carve this?
First, an honest admission. Protzen and Nair wrote that the crisp inside right angles were most likely not made with hammerstones. Inca stonework has rounded inner corners. Tiwanaku does not.
And no construction tools have been identified at the site. So the experts themselves said: we do not know exactly how they did it. Remember that, because it is true.
So Stella Nair ran an experiment. She tested blades, flakes and thin chisels of flint, agate, jasper, obsidian, quartzite and hematite on hard andesite. Bronze tools barely worked.
With stone tools, she carved a half-cross design about twenty centimetres across, with the same precision as the carvings at Puma Punku.
It took forty hours, including trial and error. The researchers estimated an experienced carver would need about twenty-five.
But one thing she could not reproduce: the perfectly flat inside surface of the carving. That part is still an open question, and we mark it as unsolved.
Now scale it up. A state of tens of thousands of people, organised labour, years of work, and specialists repeating the same shapes over and over.
Grinding with sand and flat stones, checking with straight edges, repeating a proven template. Slow, but entirely human.
Station six. The alien hypothesis, tested claim by claim.
The modern version starts in nineteen sixty-eight, with Erich von Däniken's book Chariots of the Gods. Television picked it up and made Puma Punku a star.
On one episode, Giorgio Tsoukalos said Puma Punku is the only site on Earth that, in his opinion, was built directly by extraterrestrials. Let's test what the evidence says.
Claim one: fifteen thousand years old. That idea comes from Arthur Posnansky, who calculated star alignments at a different building, the Kalasasaya. He assumed perfect alignment to start with.
The radiocarbon date from inside the mound says after AD five hundred and thirty-six. An assumption cannot beat a measurement. Claim one fails.
Claim two: diamond drills or lasers. A laser leaves melted, glassy rims. Machines leave regular cutting marks. Nobody has published a single measurement showing either at Puma Punku.
On the same show, Tsoukalos visited a machinist's workshop and admitted the surface looks nothing like a diamond-cut surface. His answer: it must have eroded. That is not evidence. It is an excuse.
And when David Childress held a set square against a block on camera to prove precision angles, the square did not line up. The block was out by a few degrees.
Claim three: the stones are poured concrete, a geopolymer. Joseph Davidovits published papers in twenty nineteen arguing this, using microscope samples.
But earlier petrographic and chemical work matched the stones to natural quarries, and abandoned blocks sit on the route from those quarries. Casting is not needed. The claim stays fringe.
Claim four: Puma Punku was a lake port. Lake Titicaca drains out about thirty metres below Tiwanaku, and its highest levels kept the shore many kilometres away. No port.
And then the strongest test of all. In twenty eighteen, Vranich modelled one hundred and forty andesite pieces and seventeen sandstone slabs, and 3D printed them at four percent scale.
The whole model cost about twelve hundred dollars. When a building was put back together, its design was immediately recognisable from older sites nearby, like Chiripa and Pukara.
Puma Punku has local ancestors. The design grew out of Andean building traditions. Vranich called that a solid piece of evidence against the alien claim.
Survey complete. Here is the report.
Built by Tiwanaku, after AD five hundred and thirty-six: evidence. Stone from known local quarries: evidence. Standardised, prefabricated H-blocks: evidence. Identical, machine-perfect blocks: false.
Hand tools match the carving: partly, with the flat inner faces still unsolved. Eight-hundred-ton stones and a fifteen-thousand-year date: debunked. Lasers and alien builders: no evidence at all.
The verdict. Puma Punku is not a crash site of alien technology. It is a masterpiece of engineering by the people of Tiwanaku, with standard parts, metal cramps and scale models.
There is still a real mystery here: exactly which tools made those flat inner faces. That is a question for archaeology, not for spaceships.
And giving the credit to aliens takes it away from the people who earned it. The ancestors of the Aymara built this, fourteen hundred years ago.
That is the survey. More ancient mysteries are waiting, from the stars to the stones.
Subscribe so you do not miss the next case. And tell us in the comments: if you could take one instrument to Puma Punku, what would you measure first?
